meta.subtitle: A wide-moat payments network compounding volume into cash and buybacks, priced at a premium under a live interchange overhang

advisories: model vs Street expected return diverge by 33pp — informational, not scored

analystSentiment.commentary: Visa runs VisaNet, the network that authorizes, clears and settles payments among consumers, issuers, acquirers and sellers across more than 200 countries and territories. It is paid for moving money, not for lending it. Net revenue rose {+14%+} to $11,633 million in the quarter ended June 30, 2026 and {+15%+} over the nine months, which the MD&A attributes primarily to growth in nominal cross-border volume, nominal payments volume and processed transactions, partially offset by higher client incentives. Operating expenses grew faster than revenue in that quarter, a cost trend the financials section weighs against the stronger nine-month results. Cash generation and capital return remain the core of the case. Against them stand a premium multiple and fee regulation and litigation that the risk section sets out. We rate V **HOLD** with a $345–$455 target range. Our probability-weighted fair value is $401.00, an expected upside of +8.9% from $368.29.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Visa Inc., founded in 1958 and headquartered in San Francisco, is a payments technology company. It operates VisaNet, which provides authorization, clearing and settlement, and it offers credit, debit and prepaid card products; tap to pay, tokenization and click to pay; Visa Direct for money movement; acceptance solutions; risk detection and prevention solutions; and advisory and other services. Its brands are Visa, Visa Electron, V PAY, Interlink and PLUS, and it serves consumers, sellers, financial institutions and government entities. The 10-Q is explicit that Visa is not a financial institution: it does not issue cards, extend credit or set rates and fees for account holders of Visa products.

Revenue comes from four lines, reported net of client incentives. Service revenue follows payments volume, data processing revenue follows processed transactions, international transaction revenue grows with cross-border volume, and other revenue includes Advisory and Other Services. Visa reports as a single segment, so this report reads the business at the consolidated level. The fiscal year ends September 30, and FY25 net revenue was $40.0B. At $368.29 the market values the company at about $691.4B.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: Visa is a wide-moat network whose earnings compound through volume, pricing and a shrinking share count, and the question is how much of that a premium price already pays for. On the bull side, revenue has grown in every year of the five-year table, the nine months to June 2026 grew faster than FY25 did, and the business turns most of its revenue into cash that it hands back to shareholders. On the bear side, the June quarter's operating expenses outgrew revenue, trailing margins sit below their FY21–FY24 level, and the fees Visa's volume depends on are under regulatory and legal pressure in the U.S. and abroad. Our Base case is that consensus earnings arrive and the multiple eases, which puts the shares near the Street's target. Set against a Bear case that prices a fee-rule shock and a slowdown together, the expected return falls short of the BUY line, and our fair value sits below the consensus. We rate the shares HOLD: a business worth owning, at a price that already pays for most of the good outcome.

catalysts: Fiscal 2026 closes on September 30, and the year-end results test the consensus path the growth section lays out.
Repurchases under the April 2026 authorization keep reducing the share count, a lever the capital-allocation discussion weighs at today's price.
International revenue growing faster than U.S. revenue shifts the mix abroad, as the growth section details.
Other revenue, which the MD&A ties to Advisory and Other Services and select pricing modifications, adds a source of growth beyond card volume.
risks: U.S. debit interchange: a 2025 court ruling against Regulation II could, if it prevails on appeal, lead to a significantly lower debit cap.
Interchange litigation keeps generating accruals whose final cost could differ from the escrow deposits.
Costs: operating expenses and client incentives both grew faster than net revenue in the June quarter.
Valuation: at a premium multiple, a fee-rule shock combined with a slowdown would take the shares below their 52-week low, the outcome the Bear case prices.
Consumer spending and cross-border travel drive volume, and both weaken in a slowdown.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended September 30.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Net revenue has risen in every year of the five-year table, from $24.1B in FY21 to $40.0B in FY25, when it grew {+11.3%+}. Profitability did not keep pace in FY25. Operating margin sat between 64.2% and 65.7% from FY21 to FY24, then fell to 60.0% as operating income edged up to $24.0B from $23.6B. The captured excerpts give no reason for the FY25 step-down, so we assign none. On a trailing basis the operating margin is 60.7% and the net margin 50.8%, close to the FY25 level rather than back in the earlier band.

The quarter ended June 30, 2026 shows the same pressure. Net revenue rose 14%, but operating expenses rose {-19%-} to $4,756 million, which the MD&A attributes primarily to higher personnel expenses; the quarter's operating margin was 59.1%. GAAP net income grew {+7%+} to $5,628 million and diluted EPS {+10%+} to $2.97. The nine months were stronger: net revenue reached $33,764 million against operating expenses up 13%, net income rose to $17,502 million and diluted EPS rose 20% to $9.14. In both periods EPS grew faster than net income, reflecting a lower diluted share count that the repurchases discussed under capital allocation most likely explain.

Visa also reports non-GAAP results: diluted EPS of $3.32 in the quarter, up 11%, and $9.79 for the nine months, up 15%. Non-GAAP operating expenses rose 17% in both periods, which the MD&A ties primarily to higher marketing and personnel expenses. The reconciliation is not in the captured excerpt, so we do not say which items separate the two bases.

We read the income statement as a strong revenue engine carrying a cost base that has lately grown faster than it. Our Base case assumes margins hold near the trailing level rather than return to the FY21–FY24 band.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended September 30.

financials.balanceCommentary:
At FY25 Visa held $17.2B of cash and short-term investments against $25.2B of total debt, for net debt of $8.0B, with total debt up from FY24. These are fiscal-year-end figures and predate the $3.0 billion of fixed-rate senior notes issued in February 2026, with maturities ranging between 3 and 10 years. On trailing figures, net debt/EBITDA is 0.4x and interest coverage is 34.8x, so debt service places no meaningful claim on earnings.

Total equity has stayed between $35.6B and $39.1B across the five years, even as net income ran between $12.3B and $20.1B a year. The earnings have gone out to shareholders rather than building up on the balance sheet.

The current ratio fell from 1.75 at FY21 to 1.08 at FY25 and is 0.99 on a trailing basis. The pack does not break out the current liabilities behind that decline, so we draw no conclusion on its cause. With coverage this high we treat a current ratio just under 1 as an item to monitor rather than a liquidity problem.

The balance sheet can keep funding returns and occasional acquisitions. It is a thinner cushion than the FY21 figures suggest, because debt has risen and the current ratio has tightened.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended September 30.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
FY25 operating cash flow was $23.1B and capital expenditure $1.5B, leaving free cash flow of $21.6B and an FCF margin of 53.9%. That margin ran between 60.2% and 61.0% from FY21 to FY23, dropped to 52.0% in FY24 and has only partly recovered. Operating cash flow fell in FY24, to $20.0B from $20.8B, while revenue grew, and no captured document explains the decline. Capital expenditure has risen each year but remains small against operating cash flow, which is what makes the model so cash-generative.

Capital return has grown in every year of the table. Share repurchases rose from $8.7B in FY21 to $18.3B in FY25, and dividends from $2.8B to $4.6B. Together, FY25 buybacks and dividends exceeded FY25 free cash flow.

We read this as a very large cash engine that no longer converts at its FY21–FY23 rate and pays out everything it generates. The return program depends on cash flow staying at least this strong.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
At $368.29 Visa trades at the vendor's 31.3x trailing P/E, 15.5x sales and 24.8x EV/EBITDA, with a trailing FCF yield of 3.0% and a dividend yield of 0.73%.

Two forward multiples appear in the pack. The 27.8x labelled next-twelve-months matches the price against FY26E EPS of $13.23, for a fiscal year that ends September 30, 2026, days after the price date, so it is in effect a current-year multiple. We use the ~24.5x on FY27E EPS of $15.00 as our forward anchor. The pack does not state whether consensus EPS is GAAP or non-GAAP, so we do not compare FY26E EPS with FY25 GAAP diluted EPS of $10.20 as if the two were on the same basis.

There is no peer column in the pack, so we judge the multiple against Visa's own economics rather than against competitors. That forward multiple is a premium. For a business with the margins and cash conversion the financials section shows, it is a defensible one, but it leaves little room for a step-change in fee regulation, the shock the Bear case prices.

Analysts are firmly positive. Of 40 covering the stock, 36 rate it Buy, 3 Hold and 1 Sell, for a Strong Buy consensus. The consensus target is $419.36 (+13.9%), the median $422.00 and the range $330.00–$466.00.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Volume keeps growing at double digits, the June quarter's cost growth eases, and fee regulation stays a slow overhang. Applying today's 31.3x trailing multiple to FY27E consensus EPS would put the shares near the $466.00 high Street target. We set Bull a little below it, because the regulatory cases stay open even in this outcome.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Consensus is delivered on both FY26E and FY27E EPS, with margins near the trailing level and litigation accruals continuing. The 27.8x current-year multiple (the one labelled next-twelve-months) holds a year out and is applied to FY27E consensus EPS, which puts the price in line with the consensus target and median.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: A regulatory step-change, such as a significantly lower U.S. debit cap after the Regulation II appeals or U.S. credit-routing legislation, or a heavier litigation outcome, arrives alongside a consumer slowdown. EPS stalls near the FY26E consensus for a year instead of rising toward FY27E, and the multiple falls from the ~24.5x forward anchor into the low twenties. The price sits below the $293.89 52-week low, which the shares reached in the past year without any of these shocks.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
Weighted, the cases contribute $135.00 (Bull), $210.00 (Base) and $56.00 (Bear), for a fair value of $401.00. That is an expected upside of +8.9% against a Bear-case downside of -24.0%, a reward/risk of 0.37×, which derives HOLD.

The Bear weight is the deciding call. The case for 20%: the November 2025 10-K described a live dispute over Regulation II, with one district court vacating the debit-cap standard and another upholding the Federal Reserve's discretion, and it still described a Federal Reserve proposal issued in October 2023 only as a proposal. Interchange accruals continued through the nine months to June 2026, and the June quarter showed earnings lagging revenue without any shock. The case for less: the Bear needs a fee shock and a slowdown together, and the nine months delivered revenue growth of 15% with diluted EPS growing faster still. We keep that weight because the Regulation II outcome alone could move the fee economics, but the weight is a judgment, not a finding. That Bear weight is why our fair value sits below the consensus target. No Street target sits as low as this case; the lowest is $330.00.

The HOLD is a close call on the weights: moving roughly a third of the Bear weight to Bull derives BUY. Nor does the label rest on the September 21 close. On the 30 closes from August 7 to September 18 shown on the price chart, the same scenarios derive HOLD on all but two mid-August sessions, August 12 and August 17, which derive BUY. The shares rose in late August and then drifted back, and no captured source explains either move. The $345–$455 target range brackets the Base case.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Visa reports one segment, so the revenue lines are the useful view. In the quarter ended June 30, 2026, service revenue rose 14% to $4,922 million, data processing revenue 17% to $6,042 million, international transaction revenue 6% to $3,853 million and other revenue 45% to $1,496 million. Client incentives of $4,680 million, up 18%, are deducted to reach net revenue of $11,633 million. The MD&A gives a driver for each line: nominal payments volume for service revenue, processed transactions for data processing, nominal cross-border volume excluding transactions within Europe for international transaction revenue, and Advisory and Other Services for other revenue. International transaction revenue grew far more slowly than the cross-border volume behind it, which the MD&A ties to lower volatility of a broad range of currencies and business mix. Client incentives grew faster than net revenue, a cost the risk section takes up.

moatFactors.name: Two-sided network
moatFactors.body: VisaNet connects issuing and acquiring financial institutions, sellers and consumers in more than 200 countries and territories, and it handled 71,662 million processed transactions in the June quarter. Each additional cardholder makes acceptance more valuable to sellers, and wider acceptance makes the cards more valuable to holders, so an entrant has to win both sides at once. The network's reach does not, however, protect the fee charged on each transaction, which regulators can act on directly.

moatFactors.name: Pricing power
moatFactors.body: The MD&A names select pricing modifications as a driver of growth in service, data processing and other revenue, in both the June quarter and the nine months. That is evidence Visa can still raise prices on parts of its book. The power is checked on two sides: client incentives rise with payments volume, and interchange regulation, covered in the risk section, bears on the fees that make Visa products attractive to issuers.

moatFactors.name: Global reach and services
moatFactors.body: Global reach lets Visa carry cross-border ecommerce and travel-related spending, and the MD&A credits value-added services and a higher cross-border transaction mix for part of the growth in data processing revenue. This part of the moat earns more in some years than others: cross-border flows are tied to travel, and international transaction revenue depends on currency volatility as well as on volume.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat WIDE. The two-sided network, the pricing the MD&A describes and the global reach are structural, and revenue has grown in every year of the five-year table despite the regulatory actions the 10-K lists. We do not see a competitor displacing the network as the main threat. The threat is to the price of using it: interchange caps, routing rules and litigation act on the fees around each transaction, and the margins the financials section shows have not returned to their earlier band. The moat protects the volume; it does not guarantee the margin on that volume, and our valuation leans on both.

points: Service revenue in the June quarter rested on nominal payments volume growth of 11%, measured on the March quarter because service revenue is assessed on the prior quarter's volume. U.S. payments volume grew 8% and international payments volume 15%, both nominal; in constant dollars, Visa-wide and international growth were lower.

Processed transactions, the primary driver of data processing revenue, rose 10% in the June quarter and 9% over the nine months. Nominal cross-border volume, excluding transactions within Europe, grew 14% in the quarter.

International net revenue rose 16% to $7,223 million in the June quarter against 12% for the U.S., to $4,410 million, so the mix is shifting abroad. The constant-dollar gap noted above shows that part of that shift is currency rather than activity.

Consensus expects FY26E revenue of ~$45.8B (+14%) and FY27E revenue of $50.8B, with EPS of $13.23 and $15.00. Nine-month revenue growth is running slightly ahead of the FY26E pace, so the FY26 figure looks achievable. FY27E implies slower revenue growth, and EPS growth that year will depend on costs and repurchases.

Growth depends on the consumer. The MD&A attributes volume growth primarily to continued resilience in consumer spending and ongoing expansion in digital commerce, with ecommerce growing faster than face-to-face spend, and says the extent to which these trends support volume will depend on consumer spending levels and broader macroeconomic conditions. A slowdown would reach revenue through all three volume drivers at once.

management.leadership: Visa's December 2025 proxy names Ryan McInerney as Chief Executive Officer, Chris Suh as Chief Financial Officer, Rajat Taneja as President, Technology, Kelly Mahon Tullier as Vice Chair, Chief People and Corporate Affairs Officer, and Paul Fabara as Chief Risk and Client Services Officer; the pack has nothing later on the team. For fiscal 2025, 95% of the CEO's target total direct compensation was variable and at-risk, and an average of 91% for the other named executives. Performance shares vest after a three-year performance period based on EPS and relative TSR, stock options and restricted stock units vest annually over three years, and payouts are capped at 200% of target. The annual cash incentive uses a scorecard whose financial goals are Net Revenue Growth, Net Income Growth and EPS Growth, each on a "VIP adjusted" basis, and the proxy says actual performance exceeded the financial goals for fiscal 2025. We see the structure as well aligned with per-share value. The weak point is the adjusted basis: the excerpt does not define the adjustments, so a holder cannot tell whether litigation accruals count against management's pay.
management.capitalAllocation:
Repurchases dominate. In April 2026 the board authorized a $20.0 billion share repurchase program, and in the nine months to June 30, 2026 Visa bought back 50 million class A shares for $16.5 billion, already close to the full-year FY25 amount; $28.4 billion of authorization remained at June 30, 2026. In February 2026 the company paid $1.5 billion in cash for Prisma Medios de Pago S.A.U. and Newpay S.A.U. in Argentina.

Repurchases are a sound use of cash for a business with low reinvestment needs. At the premium the valuation section describes, though, each dollar retires fewer shares than it would at a lower multiple, and the cash-flow discussion shows returns already exceed free cash flow. The Argentine deal carries a regulatory question: the 10-K lists Argentina among the Latin American countries that have adopted or are exploring interchange caps. The excerpt gives no return target for the deal, so we treat it as a modest bet on a market with its own fee risk.
management.governance: The captured proxy excerpt, dated December 2025, is the compensation discussion only. It carries no board composition, independence or related-party disclosure, so we make no claim about the board. The share structure changed during the period: in May 2026 Visa accepted 3 million class B-1 and 120 million class B-2 shares tendered in an exchange offer and issued 61 million class B-3 and 23 million class C shares. The excerpt does not give the voting or conversion terms of these classes, so we cannot say what the exchange means for class A holders. Nothing in the captured material points to a controlling holder. For outside holders, the governance question here is less about control than about the adjusted pay metrics discussed under leadership.
management.insiderOwnership: The excerpt includes no beneficial-ownership table, so we state no insider or group stake. Executives' exposure to the share price comes through the equity awards described under leadership; how many shares they hold outright is not in the pack.

idiosyncratic: U.S. debit interchange. As of the November 2025 10-K, Federal Reserve rules capped U.S. debit interchange for large financial institutions at 21 cents plus 5 basis points per transaction, plus a possible 1-cent fraud adjustment, and an October 2023 proposal would lower it further. In August 2025 a North Dakota court vacated the cap's standard, while a Kentucky court upheld the Federal Reserve's discretion; the 10-K said affirmation could potentially mean a significantly lower cap. Visa generally does not receive interchange, but the 10-K said changes to it can substantially affect volume and net revenue. The appeal is the regulatory event our Bear case prices most directly, and affirmation would raise our Bear weight, as the final recommendation sets out.

Credit routing and caps abroad. As of the November 2025 10-K, the Credit Card Competition Act could be reintroduced; versions from 2022 and 2023 required large issuers to offer at least two unaffiliated networks for credit. An Illinois law of May 2024 restricting interchange on tax and gratuity was under legal challenge. The EU capped consumer credit and debit interchange at 30 and 20 basis points, with another impact assessment planned; Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Costa Rica had adopted or were exploring caps; and Australia's central bank had proposed lower ones. We rank U.S. credit routing first, since U.S. consumer credit carried $644 billion of nominal payments volume in the March quarter, and the Bear case prices it. The foreign caps we treat as incremental, inside the Base case.

Interchange litigation. In the nine months to June 30, 2026 Visa recorded additional accruals of $1.1 billion for claims in the interchange multidistrict litigation and deposited $875 million into the U.S. litigation escrow account. The MD&A says the additional accruals could be higher or lower than the deposits, so the final cost remains open, and these accruals reduce GAAP earnings.

Cost growth and client incentives. In the June quarter, operating expenses grew faster than net revenue, and so did client incentives, which the MD&A says rise with payments volume. If both trends persist, revenue growth will keep turning into slower earnings growth, the pattern our Bear case extends.
risks.systemic: Visa's volume follows consumer spending and cross-border travel, and a recession would reach all of its revenue lines at once. Currency is a second channel. Exchange-rate movements added about one percentage point to net revenue growth in both the June quarter and the nine months, and the MD&A notes that exchange-rate movements and volatility have contributed to periodic variability in results and may continue to do so. The 10-K adds that regulation may increase in quantity, complexity and scope in response to heightened geopolitical tensions, with differing rules on matters such as domestic processing and localization requirements; it says complying increases costs and operational complexity and reduces revenue opportunities. Against these, debt is small relative to earnings, so a downturn would test growth and the multiple rather than solvency. We see the macro exposure as ordinary for a payments network; regulation is the larger systemic risk.

body: **HOLD, $345–$455.** Visa is a wide-moat network growing revenue faster than it did in FY25, converting most of it to cash and returning that cash to shareholders. The weighted outcome of our scenarios falls short of the BUY line, and our fair value sits below the Street, for the reasons the valuation section gives. We would keep an existing position for the compounding and wait for a better price or a clearer regulatory outcome before adding.

**What would change the call.** On these scenarios, BUY needs a price back near the mid-August lows on the price chart, and a fall to that level without new information would call for a re-run. We would raise the Bear weight if the North Dakota ruling against Regulation II is affirmed on appeal, if U.S. credit-routing legislation advances, or if interchange accruals step up. We would cut it, which could derive BUY, if operating expense growth falls back below revenue growth, GAAP net income growth closes the gap to revenue growth, and the Regulation II dispute is resolved in the Federal Reserve's favor.
